column1: What is the core ontological difference between presentism and eternalism regarding time?
column2: Presentism: only the present moment exists (shifting quantifier domain). Eternalism: all moments exist with equal ontological standing in a fixed four-dimensional 'block universe', enabling constant-domain semantics.

column1: Why does presentism create difficulties for classical first-order logic, and what alternative does it favor?
column2: Because the domain of quantification shifts moment to moment (past entities no longer exist), applying excluded middle to past-tense sentences becomes problematic. This pressures presentism toward free logics or varying-domain semantics rather than fixed constant-domain Kripke frames.

column1: What three structural properties distinguish temporal domains like $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{Z}$, and $\mathbb{N}$?
column2: Discreteness vs. density, presence/absence of endpoints, and completeness (whether bounded subsets have suprema/infima within the set).

column1: Why is $\mathbb{R}$ the canonical domain for continuous dynamics, while $(\mathbb{Q}, <)$ is less suitable despite also being dense?
column2: $\mathbb{R}$ is Dedekind complete—every bounded subset has a least upper bound—guaranteeing limits and suprema exist. $\mathbb{Q}$ is dense but not complete, so bounded sets of rationals may lack rational suprema.

column1: What is the 'no backward branching' (backward linearity) axiom in branching time models?
column2: At any moment $t$, the set of moments strictly earlier than $t$ forms a unique linear past—history up to any point is single-valued—while moments strictly later may branch into multiple incompatible futures.

column1: In branching time logic, why can't a single future-tense operator $F$ capture both 'it will definitely be the case' and 'it is possible that it will be the case'?
column2: Because branching futures permit genuine indeterminacy: multiple incompatible continuations coexist at the present moment, so truth along one branch does not entail truth along all branches, requiring separate operators for necessity (all branches) vs. possibility (some branch).

column1: Formally define a tree model $\mathfrak{T}$ used in branching time semantics.
column2: $\mathfrak{T} = \langle T, \leq, V \rangle$: a non-empty set $T$ of moments, a partial order $\leq$ (reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive, non-total) satisfying backward linearity, and a valuation $V$ assigning atomic propositions to each moment.

column1: What is a Kripke structure in the context of temporal logic, and what are its three components?
column2: $\mathcal{M} = (S, \to, L)$ where $S$ is a set of states, $\to \subseteq S \times S$ is a transition relation between states, and $L: S \to 2^{\mathsf{AP}}$ labels each state with the atomic propositions true there.

column1: What historical insight connected Arthur Prior's tense logic to computer science verification, and who made it?
column2: Amir Pnueli (1977, Turing Award) recognized that Prior's tense operators could specify correctness properties of running concurrent programs, since a computation generates a sequence of states exactly like a temporal logic model.

column1: Why does special relativity force abandonment of absolute simultaneity?
column2: The invariant finite speed of light $c$ combined with the requirement that physical laws hold in all inertial frames implies that events simultaneous in one observer's frame (same $t_A$) are generally not simultaneous in another's frame (different $t_B$)—temporal coordinates are frame-dependent projections, not invariant scalars.

column1: What geometric reformulation did Minkowski introduce in 1908, and why was it necessary?
column2: Minkowski unified space and time into a single four-dimensional pseudo-Riemannian manifold (spacetime) with an invariant metric, replacing the Cartesian product of separate space and time, because simultaneity and temporal order are not absolute but depend on reference frame.

column1: What are Allen's Interval Algebra primitives, and why was it introduced over point-based temporal logic?
column2: Allen's Interval Algebra (1983) treats intervals $I=[t_s,t_e]$ as primitive temporal entities (not points), defining 13 mutually exclusive relations (before, meets, overlaps, during, starts, finishes, equals, and their inverses) to properly represent durative, extended processes that point-based logics like LTL/CTL cannot naturally express.
